name: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
summary: Plurals, much/many, and nouns with no plural form.

paragraphs: Some things can be counted one by one: a book, two books, ten books. Others are seen as a single mass that cannot be split into units: water, information, advice. English treats these two groups very differently, and that affects plurals, articles and quantity words such as many and much.

The confusing part is that a noun which is countable in your own language may be uncountable in English. You might count pieces of advice or items of furniture in your head, but in English, advice and furniture never take -s. This page shows you how to recognize each type and use it correctly.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Countable nouns can be plural (books). Uncountable nouns are never plural (information, never informations).

paragraphs: Errors such as informations, researches and advices are some of the most noticeable mistakes in IELTS essays, partly because these nouns are so common in academic topics. A single wrong plural stands out to an examiner.

Quantity words are another trap. Many, few and the number of go with countable nouns; much, little and the amount of go with uncountable ones. In Task 1, choosing correctly between these is part of describing data accurately.

Countable nouns have a singular and a plural form, and in the singular they need a word such as a, an or the in front. Uncountable nouns have only one form. They take a singular verb and are never used with a or an.
This is the core rule. No matter how much information you have, it is still information. Adding -s to an uncountable noun is one of the most frequent mistakes in IELTS writing.
Many of these nouns appear in academic topics again and again, so it helps to learn them as a group.

rows: information, research, knowledge, advice, homework, evidence

items.text: We need more informations.
We need more information.
Researches show that sleep improves memory.
Research shows that sleep improves memory.

sections.title: Rule 2: No a or an with uncountable nouns
sections.label: Rule 2: No a or an with uncountable nouns

paragraphs: Because uncountable nouns are not single units, you cannot put a or an in front of them. To talk about one unit, use a unit word such as a piece of, an item of or a type of.
You can also simply use some, or leave out the article completely.

rows: a piece of advice / some advice

sections.title: Rule 3: Many or much? Few or little?
sections.label: Rule 3: Many or much? Few or little?

paragraphs: Some quantity words work only with countable nouns, and others only with uncountable ones. Choosing the wrong one is a common slip, especially with much and many, and with less and fewer.
A few quantity words work with both types: some, a lot of, lots of, plenty of, enough and most. If you are unsure, a lot of is always safe.

items.text: There are much problems in big cities.
There are many problems in big cities.
Less people use public transport now.
Fewer people use public transport now.

sections.title: Rule 4: The number of or the amount of?
sections.label: Rule 4: The number of or the amount of?

paragraphs: In Task 1, you constantly describe quantities. Use the number of with countable nouns (things you can count) and the amount of with uncountable nouns (things you measure).
The same logic applies to other phrases: a large number of people, but a large amount of money.

items.text: The amount of people using buses has risen.
The number of people using buses has risen.

sections.title: Rule 5: Nouns that are already plural
sections.label: Rule 5: Nouns that are already plural

paragraphs: Some nouns are plural even without -s. People, police and children already mean more than one, so adding -s is wrong in normal use. Other nouns, such as clothes and goods, are always plural.
Watch out for irregular plurals too. Many common nouns do not add -s at all: child becomes children, not childs.

items.text: Many peoples think city life is stressful.
Many people think city life is stressful.
The family has two childrens.
The family has two children.

paragraphs: A few nouns can be countable or uncountable, with a change in meaning. Time is uncountable when it means minutes and hours, but countable when it means occasions. Work is uncountable when it means a job or effort, but a work is a piece of art or writing.
You do not need to memorize a long list. Just be careful with the common ones below.

rows: I have no time. (minutes and hours)
She is looking for work. (a job)
a work of art (a piece of art)

paragraphs: Numbers above one always need a plural noun: two reasons, three million people. But when a number is used as an adjective before another noun (joined with a hyphen), the noun stays singular: a ten-year plan, a five-minute walk.
Also note that million, thousand and hundred do not take -s after a number: two million people, not two millions people.

items.text: There are two main reason for this.
There are two main reasons for this.
The government announced a ten-years plan.
The government announced a ten-year plan.
The city has five millions residents.
The city has five million residents.

sections.title: Rule 8: Every and each + singular; one of + plural
sections.label: Rule 8: Every and each + singular; one of + plural

paragraphs: After each and every, use a singular noun: every student, each country. After one of, the noun is always plural, because you are choosing one from a group: one of the reasons, one of the countries.
This rule is easy to forget in longer sentences, especially with the very common phrase one of the main reasons.

items.text: This is one of the main reason for pollution.
This is one of the main reasons for pollution.
Every students must take the test.
Every student must take the test.

paragraphs: Here is how these rules appear in real IELTS writing.

rows: The amount of water used by farms fell.
The city had two million residents.
No -s on million after a number
Fewer people smoke than in the past.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common noun mistakes in IELTS essays.
Use this routine on every noun that ends in -s and every noun after a or an.

steps: Find nouns with -s and nouns after a / an.
Is the noun uncountable (information, research, advice, equipment)? Then remove the -s and the a / an.
Check the quantity word: many / few / number for countable; much / little / amount for uncountable.

furtherStudy.title: Purdue OWL: Count and Noncount Nouns
furtherStudy.description: Rules and examples for countable and uncountable nouns.

furtherStudy.title: Purdue OWL: Count and Noncount Nouns Exercises

cards.front: Can you give me some ____ about the exam?
cards.why: Advice is uncountable, so it never takes -s.

cards.front: Recent ____ shows that sleep improves memory.
cards.why: Research is uncountable, so it has no plural form and takes a singular verb (shows).

cards.front: There are too ____ cars in the city center.
cards.why: Cars are countable, so we use many.

cards.front: The ____ of water used in farming has increased.
cards.why: Water is uncountable, so we use the amount of.

cards.front: ____ prefer online shopping because it saves time.
cards.why: People is already plural, so it does not take -s.
Equipment is uncountable, so it never takes -s.

cards.front: This is one of the main ____ for the problem.
cards.why: After one of, the noun is always plural.

cards.front: The government announced a ten-____ plan.
cards.why: When a number and noun are joined to describe another noun, the noun stays singular: a ten-year plan.

cards.front: Today, ____ people smoke than twenty years ago.
cards.why: People are countable, so we use fewer. Less is for uncountable nouns.

cards.front: I bought ____ new furniture for my room.
cards.why: Furniture is uncountable, so it cannot take a. Use some or a piece of.
